label: Phage Cycles: Lytic, Lysogenic, Chronic
rows: Rapid takeover of bacterial metabolism; production of multiple copies of virus
Destruction of the host cell (viral lysozyme bursts the wall); generalized transduction: random pieces of the host DNA may be transmitted to other bacteria
Integration of viral genes as a prophage; viral genes replicated with the host cell
May acquire new traits (ability to make a toxin); immune to reinfection; specialized transduction: all cells carry the same DNA from the host
Penetration via protein compatibility (no lysozyme); virions assembled and released chronically
Bacterial growth slowed, the host not lysed; a cooperative arrangement: the host gains benefits that contribute to pathogenicity (toxins and biofilms)

rows.note: Lysogenic: adsorption and penetration are the same as in the lytic cycle; a shock of some kind induces the prophage to release and start a lytic cycle (slide 15). Chronic: filamentous phages, flexible rods with single-stranded DNA (slide 16). Slide 17: virulent phages have only lytic cycles; temperate phages have lysogenic cycles and lytic or chronic cycles.

key: lytic: the host cell is destroyed and the new virions released
lysogenic: the viral genes hide in the bacterial chromosome as a prophage
chronic: virions are released slowly while the bacterium lives on, its growth slowed
mnemonic.breaks: A lysogenic prophage does not hide forever: a shock induces it into a lytic cycle. The chronic “leak” also helps the host (toxins, biofilms).

label: Animal Virus Versus Phage Replication
rows: Adsorption, then penetration: viral lysozyme and a tail pin breach the wall and inject the viral DNA (slide 14)
Not needed: only the DNA goes in
★ Required to release the genetic material (the pH of the cytoplasm versus the extracellular fluid) (slide 22)
The bacterium becomes a viral factory: DNA first, then capsid components (slide 14)
Most DNA viruses are budded off the nucleus; most RNA viruses multiply in the cytoplasm (slide 24)
Lytic: viral lysozyme makes the host cell wall burst (slide 14); chronic: extruded without lysis (slide 16)
★ Budding, which may assist in acquisition of the envelope (slide 22)

rows.note: ★ The recording: “This you need to know.” The exception to the nucleus row: poxviruses multiply in the cytoplasm, in factory areas (slide 32).

key: entry: the whole animal virion is engulfed (a phage injects only its DNA)
uncoating is required to free the genetic material
most DNA viruses are made in, and budded off, the nucleus
release by budding, which gives the envelope (a lytic phage bursts the wall)
mnemonic.breaks: Poxviruses break “Nucleus”: they multiply in the cytoplasm. A chronic phage also leaves without bursting the cell, but it is extruded, not budded.

label: Acute, Persistent Chronic, Persistent Latent
rows: A rapid course; the lytic cycle
The virus is detectable in tissue samples, multiplying at a slow rate; symptoms mild or absent; may involve integration of the genetic material into the host chromosome
Human immunodeficiency virus; ★ hepatitis B virus

After a lytic cycle the virus enters a dormant phase: generally not detectable, no symptoms; can reactivate and result in recurrent infections. The viral DNA is an episome: in the nucleus but not integrated

rows.note: Persistent infections last many years or a lifetime; there are 2 types (slide 26). Slide 27 (possible effects on host cells): lytic infection, latent infection with recurrence, chronic infection, transformation to malignancy: “Think about the similarity of these cycles to the phage cycles.” ★ The recording: “different kinds of viral infections that you need to know”; hepatitis B is “a chronic, persistent infection, as opposed to the latent, which are the herpes viruses”.

key: acute: a rapid lytic course (colds, flu)
persistent chronic: detectable, multiplying slowly, few symptoms (human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B)
persistent latent: dormant and undetectable, then wakes as a recurrent infection (herpesviruses)
mnemonic.breaks: Hepatitis B simmers in only some patients: slide 88 says most infected eventually develop immunity and a small number develop chronic liver disease.

label: Oncogenic Versus Teratogenic Viruses
rows:
Epstein-Barr virus: Burkitt’s lymphoma
Herpesvirus 8: Kaposi’s sarcoma
Hepatitis B: hepatic carcinoma
Papillomaviruses: cervical and penile cancer
Several viruses cross the placenta, causing developmental disturbances and permanent defects

rows.note: Her chart (slide 5) gives herpes simplex 2 an “association with cervical and penile cancer; often diagnosed with Pap smear”; slide 28 gives cervical and penile cancer to the papillomaviruses, and slide 99 ties the Pap smear to human papillomavirus. Not resolved here.
Burkitt lymphoma’s patients: her chart (slide 6) says “primarily affects African boys 5–7”; slide 77 says “central African children 5–7 years old”.

mnemonic.hook: Every Kid Has Papers; Rubella and Cytomegalovirus Cross.
key: the two teratogens cross the placenta
mnemonic.breaks: “Kid” stands for the disease (Kaposi), not the virus name, and is not about children; the four oncogenic letters cover cancers, the last line the fetus.

label: The DNA Virus Groups That Infect Humans
rows:
Variola, vaccinia, molluscum contagiosum, mpox, cowpox, orf
Herpes simplex 1 and 2, varicella zoster, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesviruses 6, 7, 8
Hepatitis B
Adenovirus; JC and BK viruses; human papillomavirus

rows.note: Slide 92 lists all four nonenveloped families together; slide 30’s chart splits the parvoviruses off as the single-stranded group. Slide 86: the hepadnaviruses have an unusual genome containing both double- and single-stranded DNA.

mnemonic.hook: Wrapped: Pox, Herpes, Hepadna. Naked: Adeno, Polyoma, Papilloma. Single: Parvo.
mnemonic.breaks: Hepadnaviruses (hepatitis B) sit with the double-stranded viruses but carry partly single-stranded DNA.

label: ★ The Eight Human Herpesviruses
rows: Enters the 5th cranial nerve; latent in the trigeminal ganglion
Enters the lumbosacral spinal nerve trunk ganglia

rows.note: ★ The recording: “Put a star on this little slide.” All herpesviruses show latency and cause recurrent infection; the viral DNA forms an episome (slide 55).

mnemonic.hook: Lips, Genitals, Pox-then-Shingles, Spit glands, Kissing, Rose, Rose, Kaposi.
key: varicella zoster: chickenpox first, shingles on reactivation
Epstein-Barr virus: mononucleosis, the kissing disease (slide 75)
mnemonic.breaks: The order is slide 57’s; the slides number only herpes simplex 1 and 2 and herpesviruses 6, 7, 8. Slide 58 says herpes simplex 2 is possibly oral too, and slide 60 says whitlow can be either type.

label: Herpesviruses: How They Spread, Is There a Vaccine
rows: No, but candidate vaccines in trials
Herpes simplex 1 and 2: herpetic whitlow; herpes of the newborn
Direct contact; transmission mother to child
Respiratory droplets and contact with fluid from active skin lesions
Yes, vaccines for both chickenpox and shingles
Direct contact with infectious body fluids (saliva, blood, mucus, tears, breast milk, urine, semen, cervical secretions) or tissues
None currently available, but several in clinical trials
Direct oral contact or contact with fomites contaminated with saliva
No preventive vaccines; several therapeutic vaccines in clinical trials for Epstein-Barr virus related cancers
Saliva, sexual contact, blood transfusion, organ transplant

rows.note: ★ Herpes simplex can be spread without visible lesions: genital herpes can be transmitted in the absence of lesions (slide 59). ★ Varicella zoster is most infectious 24–48 hours before lesions develop, and shingles patients can give the unvaccinated chickenpox, not shingles (slides 68–69).
Epstein-Barr virus therapeutic vaccines: the chart says “in clinical trials”; slide 79 says “available”. Both say no preventive vaccine.

mnemonic.hook: Touch, Touch, Touch, Breath, Fluids, Spit, Spit, Spit, Spit-plus; only the Breath virus gets a vaccine.
key: whitlow and the newborn: direct contact, mother to child
varicella zoster: respiratory droplets (and lesion fluid); the only herpesvirus with a vaccine
Epstein-Barr virus: oral contact, saliva on fomites
human herpesvirus 8: saliva plus sex, transfusion, transplant
mnemonic.breaks: Varicella zoster also spreads by lesion fluid, not only breath; cytomegalovirus’s fluids include saliva.

label: The Poxviruses Side by Side
tag: Comparison · Lecture 18 · her chart, slide 4; slides 40–54
rows: Inhalation of airborne saliva; contact with material from pustules or scabs; fomites (slide 40)
★ Early rash is the stage of greatest contagion; ★ the first disease eliminated by vaccine (chart); prevented by vaccination with vaccinia virus (slide 43)
Direct contact and fomites; in the United States most commonly a sexually transmitted disease (slide 46)
Small, smooth, waxy lesions on the genital area and thighs, self-limiting; tumor-like growths of the face in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome; no vaccine (chart)
Enters through broken skin, the respiratory tract or mucous membranes; body fluids or fomites (slide 48); infected animals or humans (chart)
Fever, aches, swollen lymph nodes, then a rash from the face: macules, papules, vesicles, pustules, scabs (slide 48); ★ vaccine available, with a vaccine locator tool (slide 52)
Rodents the primary reservoirs; handling cats that interacted with rodents; traumatic injury (slide 53)
Rare in humans, usually confined to the hands; a vaccine only for animals, in Europe (slide 53)
Handling sheep and goats: feeding, shearing, bites (slide 54)
Sore mouth (contagious ecthyma) in the animals; more serious in the immunocompromised

rows.note: Her chart’s fourth row (slide 4) reads Virus “Vaccinia”, Disease “Cowpox”, with cowpox’s facts; slide 43 teaches vaccinia as the smallpox vaccine virus and slide 53 teaches cowpox as its own virus.

JYNNEOS: the chart says it “became available April 2024”; slide 44 says it was approved in 2019. Slide 52: JYNNEOS is a 2-dose series 28 days apart; ACAM2000 is a single dose with multiple needle pricks.

key: variola: smallpox, the first disease eliminated by vaccine
molluscum contagiosum: small, smooth, waxy lesions
mpox: swollen lymph nodes before the rash
cowpox: human lesions usually on the hands
orf: caught from handling sheep and goats
mnemonic.breaks: Orf’s human lesion is also on the hand (slide 54’s picture), so “Hands” alone does not separate cowpox from orf; the animal does.

label: Hepatitis B and the Nonenveloped DNA Viruses
tag: Comparison · Lecture 18 · her chart, slides 6–7; slides 87–104
rows: Contact with blood or serum, sexual contact (chart); minute amounts of blood and blood products (slide 87)
Chronic in some; liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma); a great risk to health care workers from a very low infective dose; vaccine: yes
Colds, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis, infantile gastroenteritis; type 41 hepatitis in children; vaccine for types 4 and 7 for the military
Direct contact or contaminated fomites (slide 97); including sexual contact (chart)
Common, plantar and genital warts; nine types raise the risk of reproductive cancer; ★ early detection by Pap smear; vaccines available
Body fluids, contaminated food or water; JC in early childhood, BK in adolescence (chart)
JC: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (myelin destroyed); BK: interstitial nephritis, hematuria, hemorrhagic cystitis after renal transplant; none for humans
Fifth disease: slapped face rash; ★ passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus: severe fatal anemia, hydrops fetalis; adults: polyarthropathy, red blood cell production stops; vaccine cell blank

rows.note: Hepatitis B is the odd one out here: an enveloped hepadnavirus (slide 86), placed with these because it shares her chart’s slides 6–7 with them. Slide 94 calls the adenovirus vaccine inactivated and oral.

key: hepatitis B: blood-borne; minute amounts of blood transmit it; a risk to health care workers
adenovirus: ocular and respiratory secretions; conjunctivitis
human papillomavirus: warts, and cervical cancer screening
polyomaviruses: JC the brain, BK the kidney
parvovirus B19: the slapped face rash of fifth disease
mnemonic.breaks: Adenovirus is not only the eye (colds, cystitis, gut); parvovirus B19’s worst harm is to the fetus, not the cheek.

label: Is There a Vaccine?
tag: Classification · Lecture 18 · her chart, slides 4–7; slides 43, 52–53, 69, 74, 79, 91, 94, 99
rows: Variola, mpox, varicella zoster, hepatitis B, human papillomavirus

Vaccinia, a live virus vaccine, no longer routine; JYNNEOS and ACAM2000, with a vaccine locator tool; a live attenuated vaccine for chickenpox and shingles; yeast-cloned surface antigen; Gardasil and Cervarix
Types 4 and 7, oral, for military personnel in training
Used in Europe for circus and zoo animals
Molluscum contagiosum, herpes simplex 1 and 2, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesviruses 6, 7, 8, polyomaviruses
Herpes simplex: candidates in trials or research ongoing; cytomegalovirus: hard without an animal model; Epstein-Barr virus: no preventive vaccine; polyomaviruses: none for humans
Parvovirus B19’s vaccine cell on the chart is blank

mnemonic.hook: Vaccines Make Very Healthy People; the Army gets Adeno; Cows only in the zoo; the rest get No; Parvo left blank.
key: Variola, Mpox, Varicella zoster, Hepatitis B, Papillomavirus: yes
every other herpesvirus, molluscum, the polyomaviruses
mnemonic.breaks: The “Variola” vaccine is vaccinia virus, and routine vaccination has ended. Varicella zoster is the one herpesvirus that breaks the “no” pattern of its family.
